pages.en: Direction is the language of navigation, and in aviation it must be precise. This lesson builds a clear foundation for the three norths pilots work with every day — true north, magnetic north and compass north — and explains why they do not always point the same way. True north is the geographic reference: the direction along a meridian towards the Earth's geographic North Pole. It is the basis for true directions on charts and for many navigation calculations. Magnetic north is different. It is the direction of the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field, and because the magnetic poles move over time, magnetic north is not fixed. The angle between true north and magnetic north is called variation. It is named east or west, and it changes depending on where you are on the globe. Then there is compass north: the direction your magnetic compass actually shows in the cockpit. The compass needle responds not only to the Earth's magnetic field but also to magnetic influences from the aircraft itself. That aircraft influence creates deviation, the angle between magnetic north and compass north, and it can vary with heading and configuration. The practical reason this matters is simple. Pilots fly headings, and those headings must agree with charts, clearances and aircraft instruments. If you do not apply variation and deviation correctly, small errors become track errors, and track errors become separation or terrain risks, especially in reduced visibility, complex airspace or on long legs. By the end of this section you will be able to interpret the three north references confidently, understand why they differ, and apply the standard conversion logic, so that the direction you planned matches the heading you actually fly.

pages.t: What is true north, magnetic north and variation?
pages.on: Infographic, three rows: TN definition, measurement 000–360° clockwise, importance; MN definition, difference from TN; variation definition, measurement East (+)/West (−), example 5°E = MN 5° clockwise from TN.
pages.en: True north, TN, is the geographic reference direction that points along a meridian towards the Earth's geographic North Pole. It is based on the planet's axis of rotation, so it is a stable, map-based north used in navigation. A true direction is measured clockwise in degrees from true north, from 000° through 360°. For example, a true bearing of 090° points due east and 180° due south, always referenced to the true meridian. True north matters because it is the foundation for accurate navigation: charts, meridians and many navigation calculations are anchored to the Earth's geographic grid, so true north gives a consistent reference for planning tracks, measuring bearings and keeping a correct mental picture of where the aircraft is going over the ground. Magnetic north, MN, is the direction shown by the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field — the north that a freely moving magnetic needle wants to line up with. A critical operational point is that the Earth's magnetic field is not perfectly stable. The magnetic poles move over time, so the relationship between true north and magnetic north changes as the field slowly evolves. That is why variation values on charts and in published data must be updated periodically. Magnetic north differs from true north because true north is defined by geography — the rotation axis and the geographic pole — while magnetic north is defined by the physics of the magnetic field. The angle between them is called magnetic variation, and it depends on where you are on the Earth. This difference is fundamental to converting between the true bearings on charts and the magnetic headings used by most cockpit instruments and ATC procedures. Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north at a given place. It tells you how far the direction of the Earth's magnetic field is offset from the geographic meridian, and it is the first correction you apply when converting between true directions on the chart and magnetic headings. Variation is named east or west; east variation is often written as plus and west variation as minus. So a variation of 5° east means magnetic north is 5° clockwise from true north: if you face true north, magnetic north is slightly to your right by 5°. A useful quick check: with east variation, magnetic north is to the east, right of true; with west variation it is to the west, left of true.

pages.t: True north, magnetic north and variation (summary)
pages.on: Globe with TN and MN arrows and variation angle; three panels repeating TN, MN and variation definitions; conclusion line.
pages.en: To summarise: true north, TN, is the geographic north reference — the direction along a meridian to the Earth's geographic North Pole. True bearings and tracks on charts are measured clockwise from TN. Magnetic north, MN, is the direction of the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field, the direction a magnetic compass needle lines up with; because the magnetic poles move over time, MN is not fixed. Variation is the angle between TN and MN at a specific place. It is measured in degrees east or west and is the key correction when converting between true and magnetic directions. East variation can be written as plus and west variation as minus, so 5° east variation means magnetic north is 5° clockwise from true north — facing true north, magnetic north lies 5° to your right. Quick check: with east variation, magnetic is east, right of true; with west variation, magnetic is west, left of true.
pages.th: สรุป ทิศเหนือจริง (TN) คือทิศเหนืออ้างอิงทางภูมิศาสตร์ ทิศตามแนวเมริเดียนไปยังขั้วโลกเหนือทางภูมิศาสตร์ bearing และ track จริงบนแผนที่วัดตามเข็มนาฬิกาจาก TN ทิศเหนือแม่เหล็ก (MN) คือทิศของส่วนประกอบแนวนอนของสนามแม่เหล็กโลก เป็นทิศที่เข็มทิศแม่เหล็กชี้ไป เพราะขั้วแม่เหล็กเคลื่อนที่ตามเวลา MN จึงไม่คงที่ variation คือมุมระหว่าง TN กับ MN ณ ตำแหน่งหนึ่ง วัดเป็นองศาตะวันออกหรือตะวันตก และเป็นการแก้หลักเมื่อแปลงระหว่างทิศจริงกับทิศแม่เหล็ก เขียน variation ตะวันออกเป็นบวก ตะวันตกเป็นลบได้ variation 5° ตะวันออกจึงหมายถึงทิศเหนือแม่เหล็กอยู่ตามเข็มนาฬิกาจากทิศเหนือจริง 5° หันหน้าไปทิศเหนือจริง ทิศเหนือแม่เหล็กอยู่ทางขวา 5° ตรวจสอบเร็ว ๆ variation ตะวันออก แม่เหล็กอยู่ตะวันออก ขวาของทิศจริง variation ตะวันตก แม่เหล็กอยู่ตะวันตก ซ้ายของทิศจริง

pages.en: Magnetic dip, also called inclination, is the angle between the horizontal plane and the Earth's total magnetic field at a given place. If the field were perfectly horizontal, a compass needle would stay level and respond cleanly to direction. In reality the field usually has a vertical component. At the magnetic poles dip is about 90°: the field lines are essentially vertical, so a magnetic needle is pulled strongly downward. At the magnetic equator dip is about 0°: the field is nearly horizontal and the needle tends to stay level. This matters for compass accuracy, because a conventional aircraft magnetic compass is designed to respond mainly to the horizontal component of the field. When dip becomes strong, especially at high latitudes, the vertical pull increases, making the compass more prone to tilt, sticking and larger turning and acceleration errors. That is why compass reliability generally gets worse in polar regions, why the compass magnet is pendulously suspended to reduce the effect of dip, and why aircraft rely more on other heading references, such as directional gyros and AHRS, as latitude increases.

pages.on: Definition: direction shown by a magnetic compass needle; influences: Earth's field and aircraft's field; adjustments for deviation and variation.
pages.en: Compass north, CN, is the direction your magnetic compass actually shows — the heading indicated by the compass as it lines up with the magnetic field it senses. That needle is influenced by two main sources: the Earth's magnetic field, which gives the natural reference towards magnetic north, and the aircraft's own magnetic field, created by its metal structure, electrical systems and avionics, and even by temporary factors such as current flow or equipment configuration. Because of these influences, compass readings normally need two corrections. First, deviation: the error caused by the aircraft's magnetism. It is found by a compass swing, recorded on the deviation card, and it can vary with heading. Second, variation: the difference between magnetic north and true north, which depends on geographic position and is taken from the chart. In practice you correct compass → magnetic using deviation, then magnetic → true using variation, so that the direction you fly matches the direction planned on charts and procedures.

pages.on: Infographic: isogonal lines 1°W, 0° agonic line, 1°E; chart legend "Var 1°W (2020) — annual change 4′E; 6 years × 4′ = 24′ (eastward reduction); 1°00′W − 0°24′ = 0°36′W; 2026 ≈ 0°36′W"; "Variation East, Magnetic Least — Variation West, Magnetic Best".
pages.en: We have defined variation. Now let us see how it is shown on the chart and how it changes with time. Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north. It is named east or west: easterly variation means magnetic north lies east of true north; westerly variation means it lies west. On the chart, variation is shown by isogonals. An isogonal is a line joining places of equal variation. The line joining places of zero variation is called the agonic line. To find the variation for your route, read the value of the nearest isogonal, and interpolate between two lines if necessary. To apply it, use the memory aid "variation east, magnetic least; variation west, magnetic best". With easterly variation, subtract it from true to get magnetic; with westerly variation, add it. Variation is not fixed. The magnetic pole moves, so variation changes slowly every year. For this reason the chart shows an epoch — the year the values were valid for — and an annual change. For example: variation 1° west in 2020, annual change 4 minutes east. By 2026, six years later, the change is 24 minutes east, so the variation is now about 0° 36 minutes west. Always use a current chart. If you must use a chart from an earlier epoch, apply the annual change before you use the variation.

pages.on: Infographic: what is deviation (MN vs CN, error caused by the aircraft); cause (airframe, ferrous materials, equipment, wiring, electrical systems; changes with heading and configuration); measurement (degrees E (+) / W (−), deviation card after compass swing, sample card "For N steer 358 (+2°E)…"); variation vs deviation; "Variation is OUTSIDE the aircraft, deviation is INSIDE".
pages.en: Deviation is the angle between magnetic north, MN, and compass north, CN — in other words, the error in the magnetic compass reading caused by the aircraft itself. Cause: deviation is created by the aircraft's magnetic influences, such as the airframe and ferrous materials, installed equipment, wiring and operating electrical systems. Because these effects change with heading and configuration, deviation is not the same in every direction. Measurement: deviation is expressed in degrees east (plus) or west (minus), and it is normally given to pilots on a compass deviation card after a compass swing. Variation versus deviation: variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north; it comes from the Earth's magnetic field and your geographic position, is taken from charts, and changes with position and slowly with time. Deviation is the angle between magnetic north and compass north; it comes from the aircraft's magnetism, changes with aircraft heading, and can be affected by electrical load and configuration. A simple way to remember it: variation is outside the aircraft — the Earth and your location — while deviation is inside the aircraft — its structure and equipment.

pages.t: Earth's magnetic force: H and Z
pages.on: Infographic: total force T resolved into H (horizontal, aligns the needle) and Z (vertical, causes dip); dip angle; magnetic equator H max dip 0°, mid-latitudes inclined, magnetic pole H ≈ 0 dip 90°; "Thailand is near the magnetic equator — small dip".
pages.en: At any point the Earth's total magnetic force acts along the line of force, usually at an angle to the horizontal. We can resolve this total force into two components. The horizontal component is called H; the vertical component is called Z. The angle between the total force and the horizontal is the angle of dip. The horizontal component H is the useful one: it is what pulls the compass needle towards magnetic north. The stronger H is, the more firmly and accurately the compass settles on a heading. The vertical component Z is the troublesome one. It tries to pull the north end of the needle down towards the magnetic pole. This is magnetic dip, and it is the root cause of the compass turning and acceleration errors. The balance between H and Z changes with magnetic latitude. At the magnetic equator the lines of force are horizontal: H is at its maximum and Z and dip are zero. Towards the magnetic poles H becomes weaker, Z becomes stronger and dip increases towards 90°. Thailand lies close to the magnetic equator. Dip is small and H is strong, so the compass is sensitive and its dip errors are small here.

pages.on: Infographic: sources — engine, wiring/electrical current, radios/avionics, steel structure; hard iron = permanent; soft iron = induced by Earth's field; compass swing (aircraft rotated through 360°) and deviation card (000°–330°); "Result = DEVIATION".
pages.en: An aircraft contains many sources of magnetism: the engine and its steel parts, the electrical wiring and the current flowing in it, the radios and avionics, and steel fittings in the structure all create magnetic fields close to the compass. This magnetism is divided into two types. Hard-iron magnetism is permanent. It is held by steel parts of the airframe, often acquired during manufacture, and it does not change as the aircraft turns. Soft-iron magnetism is temporary. It is induced in soft metal by the Earth's own magnetic field, so it changes as the aircraft changes heading and as it moves to a different magnetic latitude. Together these fields pull the compass needle away from magnetic north. The resulting error is called deviation, and it is different on every heading. Deviation is measured and reduced by a compass swing. The aircraft is placed on a compass base — a surveyed area clear of magnetic disturbance — and turned onto a series of headings. The engineer adjusts the compass to remove as much deviation as possible and records the remaining deviation on a deviation card, which is placed in the cockpit. A compass swing is repeated after avionics or electrical changes, after a major repair, or whenever compass accuracy is in doubt.

pages.t: The resultant field at the compass
pages.on: Infographic: Earth's field E_E + hard-iron field E_H + soft-iron field E_S = resultant E_R the compass follows; deviation card For/Steer 000/002, 090/088, 180/181, 270/272; "TRUE → ±VAR → MAGNETIC → ±DEV → COMPASS".
pages.en: Let us now put these fields together and see what the compass actually responds to. At the compass position there are three magnetic fields. The first is the Earth's field. The second is the aircraft's hard-iron field, which is permanent. The third is the aircraft's soft-iron field, which is induced by the Earth's field. These three fields add together as vectors to give one resultant field. The compass needle does not know which field is which; it simply lines up with the resultant. That is why the compass does not point exactly to magnetic north. The important point is that the aircraft's fields turn with the aircraft. When you change heading, the hard-iron and soft-iron fields swing round relative to the Earth's field, so the resultant changes direction by a different amount on each heading. This is why deviation varies with heading. The deviation card shows the correction. It usually lists "For" — the magnetic heading you want — and "Steer" — the compass heading you must fly to get it. This gives the full heading chain: start with the true heading from your plan, apply variation to get magnetic heading, and apply deviation to get compass heading — true, variation, magnetic, deviation, compass. Keep the two errors separate in your mind: variation belongs to the Earth and to your position; deviation belongs to your aircraft and to your heading.

pages.on: Three items: compass swinging; material placement; "Variation factors — note that deviation varies with aircraft heading and latitude". Compass-rose image.
pages.en: Reducing compass deviation is mainly about calibration and controlling magnetic influences inside the aircraft. One, compass swinging. A compass swing is the primary method. The aircraft is lined up on a series of known headings, usually using a compass rose or surveyed reference, and the indicated compass headings are compared with the known values. The differences are recorded as deviation, and a deviation card is produced so pilots can apply the correction in flight. The swing should be repeated after avionics changes, electrical work or major maintenance that could alter the aircraft's magnetic environment. Two, material placement. Deviation can increase if magnetic or magnetised items are placed near the compass. Keep tools, headsets with magnets, speaker magnets, handheld radios, tablets with magnetic covers and other ferrous objects away from the compass. Good cockpit discipline reduces unintended deviation that appears only when certain items are brought on board. Three, the factors to remember. It is important to separate the concepts. Deviation depends mainly on heading, because it comes from the aircraft's own magnetic fields and geometry. It can also be influenced by latitude indirectly, because the soft-iron part changes as the Earth's field changes with location, especially where dip is strong, making compass behaviour less stable. The practical takeaway is to expect deviation and compass performance to vary with heading, and to treat high-latitude operations as a condition where compass reliability can get worse. In practice the best safeguard is to keep the compass properly swung, keep magnetic items away, and cross-check heading information with other references whenever available.

pages.on: Definition: lines connecting points of equal magnetic variation; usage: determine variation for position and route.
pages.en: Isogonals are lines drawn on charts that join points with the same magnetic variation. In other words, anywhere along one isogonal the angle between true north and magnetic north is the same. They matter because variation changes with location, sometimes significantly over long routes. On aeronautical charts, isogonals let pilots quickly find the variation for a specific position or along a planned track. With that value you can convert accurately between true bearings and tracks from the chart and the magnetic headings used in the cockpit and by ATC, improving navigation accuracy and reducing heading errors.
pages.th: isogonal คือเส้นบนแผนที่ที่เชื่อมจุดที่มี magnetic variation เท่ากัน หรือก็คือ ตลอดแนวเส้น isogonal เส้นหนึ่ง มุมระหว่างทิศเหนือจริงกับทิศเหนือแม่เหล็กเท่ากัน เส้นนี้สำคัญเพราะ variation เปลี่ยนตามตำแหน่ง บางครั้งเปลี่ยนมากในเส้นทางยาว บนแผนที่การบิน isogonal ช่วยให้นักบินหา variation ของตำแหน่งหรือตลอด track ที่วางแผนได้อย่างรวดเร็ว เมื่อได้ค่านี้ ก็แปลงระหว่าง bearing และ track จริงจากแผนที่ กับ magnetic heading ที่ใช้ในห้องนักบินและโดย ATC ได้อย่างแม่นยำ เพิ่มความแม่นยำในการเดินอากาศและลดความผิดพลาดของ heading

pages.on: Four formulas: C → M: M = C ± DEV; M → T: T = M ± VAR; T → M: M = T ∓ VAR; M → C: C = M ∓ DEV.
pages.en: Here is the clean way to use these conversions, with the sign rule made explicit so you do not have to guess. The sign rule, every time: going from compass towards true, add east and subtract west — this applies to both variation and deviation. One: compass to magnetic, M = C + deviation east, or − deviation west. Two: magnetic to true, T = M + variation east, or − variation west. Three: true to magnetic, M = T − variation east, or + variation west. Four: magnetic to compass, C = M − deviation east, or + deviation west. Quick sanity check: the reverse conversion always flips the sign — that is why you see "±" one way and "∓" the other.
pages.th: นี่คือวิธีใช้การแปลงอย่างเป็นระบบ พร้อมกฎเครื่องหมายที่ชัดเจนเพื่อไม่ต้องเดา กฎเครื่องหมายที่ใช้ทุกครั้ง: เมื่อแปลงจากเข็มทิศไปทางทิศจริง บวกตะวันออก ลบตะวันตก ใช้ทั้งกับ variation และ deviation หนึ่ง เข็มทิศเป็นแม่เหล็ก M = C + deviation ตะวันออก หรือ − deviation ตะวันตก สอง แม่เหล็กเป็นจริง T = M + variation ตะวันออก หรือ − variation ตะวันตก สาม จริงเป็นแม่เหล็ก M = T − variation ตะวันออก หรือ + variation ตะวันตก สี่ แม่เหล็กเป็นเข็มทิศ C = M − deviation ตะวันออก หรือ + deviation ตะวันตก ตรวจสอบเร็ว ๆ การแปลงย้อนกลับจะกลับเครื่องหมายเสมอ จึงเห็น "±" ทางหนึ่งและ "∓" อีกทางหนึ่ง

pages.on: Compass heading 120°, deviation 2°E, variation 5°W → true heading 117° (120 + 2 − 5). Decorative arrow diagram TH 088°, VAR 10°E, MH 078°, DEV 4°E, CH 074°.
pages.en: Now a calculation. Start with compass heading 120°. Step one, compass to magnetic: deviation is 2° east, so add it. Magnetic heading = 120° + 2° = 122°. Step two, magnetic to true: variation is 5° west, so subtract it. True heading = 122° − 5° = 117°. So the final true heading is 117°, matching the combined shortcut 120° + 2° − 5° = 117°.
pages.th: มาคำนวณกัน เริ่มจาก compass heading 120° ขั้นแรก เข็มทิศเป็นแม่เหล็ก deviation 2° ตะวันออก ให้บวก magnetic heading = 120° + 2° = 122° ขั้นที่สอง แม่เหล็กเป็นจริง variation 5° ตะวันตก ให้ลบ true heading = 122° − 5° = 117° ดังนั้น true heading สุดท้ายคือ 117° ตรงกับวิธีลัดแบบรวม 120° + 2° − 5° = 117°

pages.on: True heading 240°, variation 3°E, deviation 4°W → compass heading 241° (240 − 3 + 4). Same decorative diagram as page 16.
pages.en: Next calculation: true to compass. Start with true heading 240°. Variation is 3° east, the adjustment for the Earth's magnetic field: going from true to magnetic, subtract east, so magnetic heading = 240° − 3° = 237°. Deviation is 4° west, the adjustment for the aircraft's magnetic field: going from magnetic to compass, add west, so compass heading = 237° + 4° = 241°. Final result: 240° − 3° + 4° = 241°.

pages.en: Aeronautical charts and on-board references work together to keep your heading calculations accurate. Isogonals on aeronautical charts are lines of equal magnetic variation. By reading the nearest isogonal, or the chart's printed variation information, you can find the variation for your position or along your route. That is the value you use to convert between true directions on the chart and the magnetic directions used in operations. Deviation data is not on the chart; it comes from the aircraft. It is given on the compass deviation card, which lists the compass error on different headings from a compass swing, and it corrects the compass reading back to magnetic. With both pieces — variation from the chart and deviation from the aircraft card — you can carry out the full conversion chain, true ↔ magnetic ↔ compass, and make sure the heading you plan is the heading you actually fly.

pages.on: Three items: variation changes, deviation variability, regular calibration. Compass-card images with garbled labels.
pages.en: Compass accuracy depends on managing two changing errors, variation and deviation, and on keeping the system calibrated. Variation changes because the Earth's magnetic field is not static. The magnetic poles drift over time, so the angle between true north and magnetic north at a given place slowly shifts. That is why charts publish variation values with an annual change, and why out-of-date chart data can introduce errors on longer routes. Deviation varies because it is created by the aircraft. The amount can change with heading, because the aircraft's magnetism interacts differently with the Earth's field in different orientations, and it can also shift with configuration or electrical load, especially after avionics changes, maintenance or new equipment. That is why regular calibration matters: a compass swing and an updated deviation card keep the corrections current. In day-to-day operations, good practice is to cross-check the magnetic compass against other heading references when available, and to treat any unusual disagreement as a cue to check deviation, configuration changes or the condition of the compass. The takeaway: manage variation with current chart data, manage deviation with the aircraft's deviation card, and keep accuracy through routine calibration and cross-checking.

pages.on: Four boxes: true north, magnetic north, compass north, accurate conversions. Cartoon globe with garbled text.
pages.en: True north is our fixed geographic reference, based on the Earth's rotation axis and the meridians on the chart. It is the foundation for plotting tracks and measuring bearings accurately during planning. Magnetic north is different. It is driven by the Earth's magnetic field, and because the magnetic poles slowly move over time, magnetic north is not a permanent reference. That is why we apply variation, the angle between true north and magnetic north, using the value shown on charts or isogonals for the area we are operating in. Compass north is what the aircraft's magnetic compass actually shows. It is influenced by the Earth's field and by the aircraft's own magnetic effects from structure, wiring and electrical equipment. That aircraft influence creates deviation, which varies with heading and sometimes configuration, and it is corrected using the aircraft's deviation card. When you apply these conversions correctly — true to magnetic using variation, and magnetic to compass using deviation — you make sure the heading you fly matches the direction you planned. That accuracy supports safe separation, reliable tracking and efficient navigation, especially in low visibility, complex airspace or on long legs.
